slides.title: Bits as polynomial coefficients
slides.body: GF(2^m) has 2^m elements. Each is represented by a polynomial of degree less than m, with coefficients 0 or 1. Bit i is the coefficient of x^i. Addition and subtraction use XOR because 1 + 1 = 0 modulo 2.
key_points: Addition and subtraction give the same result in characteristic 2.
Every nonzero field element has a multiplicative inverse.

slides.title: Reduce with the field polynomial
slides.body: The field is defined by an irreducible polynomial m(x) of degree m. When the current highest term has degree d ≥ m, shift m(x) by d − m and XOR it with the current polynomial. Repeat until the remainder has degree below m.
key_points: The AES field uses m(x) = x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x + 1, or {11B}.
In the AES field x^8 reduces to x^4 + x^3 + x + 1, or {1B}.
The same reduction rule applies at the project's primary degree, m = 163.

slides.title: Multiply by shifting, invert with Extended Euclid
slides.body: For each bit i of the multiplier, compute x^i times the first operand by shifting and reducing. XOR the values selected by the set bits. For an inverse, run Extended Euclid with A = (1, 0, m(x)) and B = (0, 1, b(x) mod m(x)). In each round divide A3 by B3, subtract the quotient times B from A using XOR, and shift the triples.
key_points: The Shift-and-XOR tables show the shifted values and the selected values' cumulative XOR.
If B3(x) = 1, B2(x) gives the inverse modulo m(x).
If B3(x) = 0, no inverse exists and A3(x) = gcd(m(x), b(x)).

slides.title: Try two course examples
slides.body: Load a preset to compare the field operation with its binary and algebraic forms. In the Chapter 4 preset, you can also switch to addition or subtraction to see {57} XOR {83} = {D4}.
key_points: Chapter 4 uses the degree-8 modulus {11B} to multiply {57} and {83}.
Chapter 5 uses the same modulus for the AES multiplicative inverse.
